Market Pulse is a research tool for investors who want to understand what the market is doing — not be told what to do about it. It aggregates real market data, macro indicators, and company fundamentals, runs them through deterministic analysis, and surfaces the results alongside AI-written interpretation.\n\nWe name what the market is doing. What you do about it is yours.

Every number in the app — prices, ratios, chart values, gauge readings — is computed in code from real data sources before any AI touches it. AI is used only to write the interpretive text on top of those numbers: summaries, digests, narrative reads. The numbers and the words have different origins and different reliability profiles.\n\nData refreshes on a schedule, not continuously. Most indicators update once or a few times a day; a small set of live prices update every minute during market hours.

AI-written content is labeled \"AI-generated · Not advice\" everywhere it appears. Before any AI-written text is shown, it\'s automatically checked for advice-sounding language — if flagged, it\'s removed rather than shown. AI never invents a number; it only writes about numbers that were already computed.\n\nAI can still be wrong. It can misread data, overstate confidence, or miss context. Cross-check anything that would influence a real decision.

Market Pulse collects two kinds of data:

How you use the app — which screens you visit, what you tap, how you engage. This is standard app-analytics data (via Firebase Analytics), tied to an anonymous app-install ID, not to you as a person. No name, no email, no account.

Crash reports — if the app crashes, a technical report is sent automatically including device model and OS version, used only to fix defects (via Firebase Crashlytics).

• No account or sign-in exists — we have no way to identify you.
• No financial account, brokerage, or payment information.
• No location data.
• No data from the market sources you view — those are fetched by our servers, never by your device directly.
Your theme, favorited stocks and metrics, and app settings are stored only on your device. They leave your device only if you back up your device yourself. Uninstalling the app removes them.

The market data you see comes from third-party providers (Finnhub, Yahoo Finance, FRED, and others). Those providers never receive information about you or your device — all data fetching happens server-side.
For informational purposes only, not financial advice.

Every gauge in Market Pulse turns a raw number into a colored reading through the same three steps — knowing them makes any gauge legible.

1. The raw value — a real measured number: an index level, a ratio, a yield, a percent. This is data, computed in code. The AI never sets it.

2. The band — the app sorts that raw value into a labeled zone (e.g. "Overbought," "Inverted," "Extreme Greed") using fixed cutoffs. These cutoffs are written into the code, not decided per-run. Some are standard market conventions (RSI ≥ 70 = overbought); others are the app's own reasonable lines (P/E ≥ 22 = expensive) — the glossary tells you which is which.

3. The color — the band maps to green / amber / red as a quick visual cue. Green is not "buy" and red is not "sell" — they mark where a reading sits on its own scale, nothing more. A red "Restrictive" on the Fed Funds rate just means rates are rising; whether that's good or bad for a given stock is yours to judge.

• Not every gauge reads its raw level: Market Breadth, Net Liquidity, and several macro gauges (payrolls, retail sales, Fed Funds, the 10-year) are classified by their direction of change instead. "Expanding" or "Rising" means the number moved that way recently — a different question than whether it's high or low.
• A couple are polarity-inverted: for the Fed Funds rate and the 10-year yield, a rising number shows red ("Restrictive") and a falling one green, because higher rates tighten conditions. Don't read the color as "the number went down."
• Some gauges have no color at all on certain fields (raw share counts, for instance) — those are pure data with no band, shown as a number to read directly.

The gauge names the condition. What it means for your decisions is the part only you can supply.
Two words this app uses twice

\"Positioning\" — Market Pulse uses this word for two unrelated things. On the Insights → Positioning tab, it means how three crowds are leaning (retail sentiment, futures speculators, short sellers). As an Indicators metric, \"positioning\" refers to where SPY sits in its 52-week range. Same word, different data, no relationship between them.\n\n\"Market regime\" — One is a deterministic, code-computed label (risk-on / risk-off / neutral) built from trend, breadth, volatility, and rates. The other is a phrase the AI Macro Hub may use in its own written verdict. The code-computed one is the app\'s factual classification; the AI one is narrative. They can differ, and that\'s expected.
Short-term yields above long-term = inverted — historically an early recession warning.
Price stretched more than +10% above its 200-day average, or more than -5% below it, tends to mean-revert — though a strong trend can stay stretched for a while.

Different scales, same idea: market mood. Extremes are the most informative reading and can persist for weeks. Fear & Greed and Put/Call both read contrarian — and Put/Call\'s scale runs the opposite direction of the other two, so \"more fearful\" is to the left here, not the right.
Illustrative values, not live data — see the real gauge inside the app for today\'s actual reading.

Read contrarian: extreme fear has historically coincided with periods where selling pressure was overdone, extreme greed with periods of elevated risk-taking. Neither is a timing signal on its own — both can stay at an extreme for a long time.
Reads the same way, in reverse: a high ratio means heavy put-buying (fear), a low ratio means heavy call-buying (greed). Just as capable of sitting at an extreme for weeks without anything changing.
Most useful ranked against its own recent history, not as a raw number alone — extremes in either direction have historically preceded a reversal as crowded positioning unwinds.

A widely watched but famously unreliable contrarian indicator on its own: extreme readings are sometimes read as a sign a consensus view has gotten crowded, not as confirmation that the consensus is right.
Overbought — momentum may be due for a pause, not a reversal call.

Every gauge and indicator across Market Pulse follows the same idea: a raw value gets bucketed into a plain-language read (e.g. \"Extreme Fear,\" \"Overbought,\" \"Neutral\") using thresholds defined elsewhere, not judged case by case. The definitions below come from the same glossary data the rest of the app uses — tap any gauge in the app itself for the fuller breakdown, including its current band and any gotchas specific to that metric.\n\nSome of these you can check yourself: the yield curve, RSI, and a stock\'s P/E versus its sector are standard measures you\'ll find on any financial site — use them to test what the app is showing you. Others, like the Fear & Greed Index or this app\'s own Copper/Gold ratio, are composite reads you can\'t easily rebuild from raw data — treat those as one lens, not gospel. Either way, the app names the condition; the conclusion is yours to draw.

A Few Things Worth Knowing About the Data Itself

• Market holidays and half-days: some indicators may show a stale "last close" value rather than a fresh one.
• After-hours vs. regular-hours pricing: a price shown outside market hours may reflect after-hours trading, which is typically lower-volume and more volatile than regular-hours pricing.
• Halted or delisted symbols: data for a halted or delisted symbol may be missing or frozen at its last known value.
• Delayed data: most market data is not real-time; treat displayed prices as approximate, not tradeable quotes.

Positioning shows where retail sentiment (AAII), large speculators (CFTC COT futures positioning), and short sellers (FINRA short interest) currently stand — three different lenses on who\'s leaning which way. A crowded reading in either direction has historically preceded a reversal as that positioning unwinds. None of these are predictions or recommendations; they describe current positioning, which can shift or reverse without warning. This interpretation is generated by an AI model and may not reflect current market conditions.

Posture tracks how professional money managers, institutional order flow, and system-wide liquidity are positioned beneath the surface of daily price moves — active manager equity exposure (NAAIM), dark pool accumulation (DIX), and the Fed\'s net liquidity backdrop. Like Positioning, this describes current conditions, not a forecast or recommendation. This interpretation is generated by an AI model and may not reflect current market conditions.
Tracks the average equity exposure of active money managers. 0% represents cash/short, 100% is fully invested, and >100% indicates leveraged long positioning.
% of dark pool volume, institutional buying
Measures the percentage of total dark pool volume that was institutional buying. A reading above 45% suggests heavy institutional accumulation under the surface.
Fed balance sheet − TGA − reverse repo
Calculates the actual fiat liquidity flowing through the financial system. Rising liquidity generally acts as a tailwind for equities and crypto, while falling liquidity acts as a headwind.

Weekly AAII survey of individual investor sentiment. The bull-bear spread is a classic contrarian indicator — extreme optimism or pessimism among retail investors has historically preceded a reversal.

Speculative net futures positioning as a percentage of open interest, framed against a trailing ~1-year percentile per contract. A crowded long or short reading has historically preceded a reversal as that positioning unwinds — first-pass framing, not backtested. Reflects the prior Tuesday\'s book, not the report\'s Friday release date. ES/NQ/RTY use CFTC\'s Legacy non-commercial category; DIA uses TFF\'s Leveraged Funds category instead (Dow futures aren\'t reported under Legacy) — see each contract\'s own methodology before comparing DIA directly against the other three.

FINRA-reported short interest in SPY/QQQ/IWM/DIA/RSP/MAGS as index/style-ETF proxies — not literal \'market short interest.\' Includes authorized-participant creation/redemption arbitrage flow, not purely directional bearish positioning. Settlement-date data, always roughly 8 business days stale by the time FINRA publishes it (see each instrument\'s settlement date vs. this gauge\'s fetched-at time).

Numbers, charts, and prices are computed directly from data — no AI involved.

Four tabs — Events (Weekly Playbook), Risks, Posture, and Positioning — each pairing a deterministic gauge with an AI-written synthesis of what it currently shows.

Every tab follows the same shape: computed gauges and data cards first, then one AI-written summary card below them, labeled "AI-generated · Not advice."

• Events (Weekly Playbook): the scheduled economic releases most likely to move markets this week — context on what each could signal, not a prediction of the reaction.
• Risks: a curated list of what could derail the current narrative, each scored by potential impact.
• Posture: how professional money is positioned beneath the surface — active-manager exposure (NAAIM), dark-pool accumulation (DIX), and system-wide liquidity.
• Positioning: where three different crowds stand — retail sentiment (AAII), large speculators (CFTC futures), and short sellers (FINRA).

A crowded reading in either direction is worth noticing: extremes have historically preceded reversals as that positioning unwinds — but "crowded" can stay crowded for a while. The app names where things stand; what you make of it is yours.
Tracked stocks, indices, and ETFs with a live price, a short AI-written read of their technical setup, and status pills (e.g. Overbought, Undervalued) computed from this app\'s own data.

• Status pills (RANGE BOUND, Undervalued, etc.): computed directly from price/fundamental data using fixed rules.\n• The read above them: generated by AI from the symbol\'s price trend, moving averages, volume, and valuation data, updated after each trading session — the one AI-written element on each card.\n• Deep Dive (inside a symbol\'s detail screen): a longer AI-written breakdown, generated roughly every two weeks or sooner around earnings, from an expanded set of price, fundamental, and macro-context data.
Tactical Momentum measures the short-term pulse of market sentiment and price momentum — how fast things are moving, and whether investors are fearful or complacent.

• Fear & Greed (CNN) — composite market mood, 0–100
• Put/Call Ratio — how defensively options traders are positioned
• SPY RSI 14-day — speed and size of recent price moves
• SMA Extension 200-day — how far SPY sits above/below its long-term trend
• VIX — expected 30-day market volatility

These five signals are most useful when they agree. RSI overbought (>70) alongside low Put/Call (<0.6) and calm VIX (<20) describes a complacent market with little hedging — a different picture than RSI overbought with VIX spiking above 30 (fear entering a stretched market, which tends to resolve more sharply).\n\nAgreement across signals is a stronger read than any single gauge.

• Whether Fear & Greed sustains an extreme (>75 or <25) across multiple days — brief touches mean less than a stretch\n• SMA Extension crossing +10%: price is running well ahead of its 200-day trend line\n• VIX moving from calm (<20) to elevated (>20) while RSI is still high — the combination that has historically preceded sharper pullbacks

RSI above 70 is a condition, not a sell signal — strong trends can stay overbought for weeks. Fear & Greed at an extreme doesn\'t mean a reversal is imminent; it means the crowd is leaning hard one way. VIX measures expected volatility, not direction — a high VIX says movement is expected, not which way it goes.

Scenario: Fear & Greed at 81, Put/Call at 0.55, VIX at 14, RSI at 74, SMA Extension at +12%.\n\nAll five pointing the same direction — elevated risk appetite, low hedging, price stretched above trend. Historically this kind of broad agreement has marked periods where the market was pricing in a lot of good news already. Whether that matters for what you\'re watching is yours to judge.
Systemic Risk tracks the structural stress signals beneath price — credit markets, volatility in bonds, currency strength, commodity signals, and whether the rally has broad participation.

• Yield Curve (10Y−2Y) — gap between long and short Treasury rates
• Credit Spreads — extra yield demanded for risky corporate bonds
• MOVE Index — bond-market volatility
• Copper/Gold Ratio — growth appetite vs. safety demand
• Consumer Rotation (XLY/XLP) — risk appetite in spending behavior
• Market Breadth (RSP/SPY) — equal vs. cap-weight S&P performance
• US Dollar (DXY) — dollar strength, global conditions proxy
• Crude Oil — inflation/demand signal

Systemic risk tends to show up in credit and bonds before it shows in stocks. Widening credit spreads (>3.0%), elevated MOVE (>100), and an inverted yield curve together describe a market where professionals are already pricing in stress — even when the stock price level hasn\'t moved yet.\n\nBreadth adds another layer: a narrow market (RSP lagging SPY) alongside rising credit spreads means the stress is visible in multiple dimensions simultaneously. The Copper/Gold ratio and Consumer Rotation confirm whether the broader economy is leaning toward growth or defense.

• The yield curve crossing zero (inversion) — historically the most watched recession warning\n• Credit spreads moving above 3.0% (Caution) or 4.0% (Stress) — the bond market repricing default risk\n• Breadth narrowing (RSP consistently lagging SPY) while indices are flat or rising — a rally carried by fewer and fewer stocks

An inverted yield curve predicts a slowdown, not its timing — the gap between inversion and any economic impact has varied from months to over a year. The Copper/Gold and Consumer Rotation ratios are this app\'s own composite lenses, not named Wall Street indicators — treat them as directional, not precise. A strong dollar is a headwind, not a verdict.

Scenario: yield curve at −0.4% (Inverted), credit spreads at 3.8% (approaching Stress), MOVE at 115 (Elevated), breadth Narrowing.\n\nFour different signals from different parts of the market pointing toward stress simultaneously. None guarantees an outcome — but when credit, rates, volatility, and breadth all move the same direction, the market is pricing in something. What you make of it is yours.
Valuation asks whether the price being paid for the market is reasonable relative to what it earns, owns, and yields — and compared to the alternative of holding risk-free Treasuries.

• P/E Ratio (TTM) — price per dollar of trailing earnings
• Price-to-Book — price relative to net asset value
• Equity Risk Premium — earnings yield vs. the 10-year Treasury
• Dividend Yield — income return on the index

These four measures tell the same story from different angles — read them for agreement, not individually. A high P/E alongside a low dividend yield and a shrinking ERP (below 2.0%) describes a market where equities offer little premium over Treasuries and price a lot of future growth already. When P/B also sits in Premium territory (>4.5x), all four are confirming the same \"richly priced\" read.\n\nThe ERP is the most useful single number here — it anchors valuation to the real alternative (Treasuries) rather than to history alone.

• ERP falling below 2.0% — the Dangerous zone where equities offer very little premium over the risk-free rate\n• P/E above 22 alongside rising 10-year yields — multiple compression risk (valuations come under pressure when rates rise)\n• All four gauges in their stretched zones simultaneously — rare, but a strong read when it happens

A low P/E is not automatically cheap — it frequently means the market has already priced in a real concern. Valuation tells you what\'s priced in; it says nothing about when or whether price corrects. These are SPY-level figures, not individual stock valuations. The P/B and dividend yield are blunter tools for a modern index than historically (much S&P value is now intangible).

Scenario: P/E at 24 (Expensive), ERP at 1.6% (Dangerous), dividend yield at 1.3% (Low), 10-year yield rising.\n\nAll four pointing rich — and rates rising means the ERP is compressing further in real time. This describes a market pricing in significant future earnings growth with little margin of safety versus Treasuries. What you conclude from that picture is yours.

Macro Vitals tracks the economy\'s underlying health — inflation, jobs, growth, and the policy rate that sits above all of it. These are the numbers that drive what the Fed does next, which in turn drives everything else.

• CPI YoY — headline inflation vs. a year ago
• Core PCE YoY + MoM — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, annual + monthly
• Unemployment Rate — jobless rate trend
• Nonfarm Payrolls — monthly net jobs added/lost
• Real GDP — inflation-adjusted economic growth (quarterly)
• Retail Sales MoM — consumer spending pulse
• Federal Funds Rate — the Fed's policy lever (polarity inverted: rising = red)
• 10-Year Treasury Yield — market-set benchmark rate (polarity inverted)

The macro picture is a sequence, not a snapshot. Start with inflation (CPI + core PCE) — it sets what the Fed is likely to do. Then jobs (unemployment + payrolls) — a strong labor market lets the Fed stay tighter longer; a weakening one raises the odds of cuts. GDP and retail sales confirm whether the real economy is absorbing the rate environment.\n\nThe 10-year yield is the market\'s real-time vote on where all of this is heading — it moves before the Fed does. Watch for divergence: if payrolls are strong but retail sales are falling, the consumer may be weakening before it shows in job numbers.

• Core PCE MoM accelerating while YoY is still falling — the monthly rate turns before the annual one, earliest inflation signal\n• Unemployment rising from a low base — even a 0.3–0.5% move off a trough has historically been an early slowdown tell\n• 10-year yield moving in the opposite direction to Fed Funds — the market pricing a policy shift before it happens

These are monthly and quarterly figures — a flat line in the app is the release cadence, not stale data. GDP is quarterly; payrolls and CPI are monthly; the 10-year moves continuously. The Fed Funds and 10-year yield colors are polarity-inverted: red means rising (more restrictive), green means falling — don\'t read the color as \"the number went down.\" One strong payrolls print doesn\'t reverse a trend.

Scenario: Core PCE MoM reaccelerating (Hot), unemployment ticking up two months in a row, 10-year yield falling while Fed Funds holds flat.\n\nInflation reaccelerating while the labor market softens and the bond market starts pricing cuts — three signals pointing in different directions. The market is betting the Fed pivots before inflation is fully solved. Whether that bet is right is the question worth watching.

Posture reads how professional and institutional money is positioned beneath the surface of price — not what the market is doing, but what the people running large pools of capital are doing about it.

• NAAIM Exposure Index — active fund managers\' actual equity exposure\n• Dark Pool Index (DIX) — buy-side share of institutional off-exchange volume\n• Net Liquidity (Fed balance sheet − TGA − Reverse Repo) — system-wide cash

Posture is deliberately not price-based — that\'s what makes it useful. The most informative read is divergence: when NAAIM is low (managers defensively positioned) but DIX is rising (institutions quietly buying off-exchange), the surface narrative and the actual behavior are pointing in different directions.\n\nNet Liquidity provides the macro plumbing context — expanding liquidity has historically been a tailwind for risk assets regardless of sentiment. All three agreeing (managers cautious + DIX accumulating + liquidity expanding) describes a setup where the professional positioning backstory is more constructive than the headlines.

• NAAIM below 40 (Extreme Fear/Hedged) with DIX above 45 (Accumulation) — the clearest manager-vs-institutional divergence signal\n• Net Liquidity direction flipping from Expanding to Draining — a slow-moving signal but meaningful when it persists\n• NAAIM above 100 (leveraged long) — managers have no dry powder left to push higher from here

NAAIM is a weekly survey with a lag — it describes positioning as of last week, not today. Net Liquidity classifies by direction with no dead-band — a tiny move still reads Expanding or Draining, so a single flip means less than a sustained trend. DIX accumulation doesn\'t mean institutions are right; it means they\'re buying. The band cutoffs on all three are this app\'s own (not-backtested) — treat them as directional, not precise thresholds.

Scenario: NAAIM at 38 (Extreme Fear), DIX at 47 (Accumulation), Net Liquidity Expanding.\n\nActive managers are heavily hedged while dark-pool institutional buying is elevated and system liquidity is growing. Three signals pointing toward a constructive backstory beneath a fearful surface. Whether that divergence resolves the way it has historically is the question — the app shows you the gap; the conclusion is yours.

Positioning tracks where three distinct crowds stand — retail investors, large futures speculators, and short sellers — each on their own timescale. The value is in seeing where they agree or diverge.\n\nNote: this is different from the \"positioning\" metric in Indicators (which tracks SPY\'s 52-week range). Same word, different data.

• AAII Bull-Bear Spread — weekly retail investor sentiment survey\n• CFTC COT Net %OI + Percentile — large speculator futures positioning (S&P, Nasdaq, Russell), raw and vs. recent history\n• FINRA Short Interest — shares sold short, days to cover, MoM change

The three crowds move on different timescales and with different motivations — retail (AAII) is weekly and emotional, futures speculators (COT) are professional and leveraged, short sellers (FINRA) are committing capital to a specific directional bet.\n\nThe most informative reads are extremes and divergences: retail at peak bearishness (read contrarian) while the COT percentile shows speculator longs near historic highs describes two crowds pulling in opposite directions. When all three are crowded the same way, the risk of an unwind grows — a crowded trade is a fragile one.

• AAII at an extreme (very high bullish or very bearish spread) — historically a contrarian signal, though it can persist\n• COT percentile above 80 or below 20 — speculator positioning at an extreme relative to its own recent history\n• Short interest days-to-cover rising while price is also rising — potential squeeze setup building

AAII is famously unreliable as a timing tool — extreme readings have preceded reversals, but the lag varies enormously. COT data is released Friday for Tuesday\'s positions — it\'s inherently lagged. FINRA short interest is twice-monthly; treat it as a slow-moving backdrop, not a real-time read. The app reports raw short shares and month-over-month change, not short-%-of-float (that data isn\'t available from this source).

Scenario: AAII spread at −35% (very bearish retail), COT percentile at 22 (speculators near historically light longs), short interest days-to-cover rising.\n\nAll three crowds leaning the same direction — defensively. Historically, this kind of broad crowd agreement on the bearish side has been a contrarian data point worth noting. Whether it is here is yours to judge.

Stock Analysis synthesizes price trend, technical setup, valuation, and macro context for individual stocks into a plain-language read updated after each trading session and a deeper dive every two weeks.

• Setup classification (Momentum / Mean Reversion / Ranging / Warning)
• SMA trend (50-day and 200-day relative to price)
• Key levels (support/resistance from recent price history)
• Valuation (P/E vs. sector median — sector-relative, not market-wide)
• Macro alignment (whether the stock's setup aligns with the macro regime)
• Forward calls (how previous setups actually resolved over 5 sessions)
• Daily digest (end-of-day AI summary, news + price action)
• Deep dive (biweekly extended analysis across trend, valuation, scenarios)

Start with the setup classification — it frames everything else. A Momentum setup in a risk-on macro regime, with price above both moving averages and sector-relative P/E not at an extreme, is a coherent picture. The same Momentum setup in a risk-off regime with stretched valuation introduces tension — the setup and the backdrop are pulling in different directions.\n\nKey levels give you the specific price context; forward calls give you the honest record of how similar setups have resolved in this stock before.

• Whether the setup classification and the macro regime agree or conflict — alignment is cleaner; conflict raises the question of which one is right\n• How previous forward calls resolved — a stock with a strong completion rate on Momentum calls is a different proposition than one where those calls have historically faded\n• Sector-relative P/E diverging sharply from the absolute P/E — the stock can look cheap vs. the market and expensive vs. its peers

The setup classification names a condition in price behavior — it is not a prediction of what comes next. \"Momentum\" means the stock has been trending; it says nothing about whether the trend continues. The deep dive is AI-written from the available data — it can miss context, misread a conflicting signal, or overstate confidence. Cross-check anything in the deep dive against the underlying numbers on the same screen.

Scenario: a stock classified Momentum, price above both SMAs, P/E 10% below sector median, macro regime risk-on, last three forward calls all completed positive.\n\nAll the signals a Momentum read would want to see are present. The forward-call history shows this specific stock has followed through before in similar conditions. Whether it does again is the question — the app shows you the setup, the conclusion is yours.

Price levels where buying or selling has repeatedly shown up — the idea being that enough market participants remember those levels that behavior tends to repeat near them. The 200-day SMA is the single most-watched support level on any major stock or index. \"Holding\" a level means price approached it and buyers stepped in. \"Breaking\" it means the level failed and the next one becomes relevant. Neither is permanent — levels get broken regularly.

The SMA Extension gauge shows how far SPY sits above or below its 200-day. The Key Levels section on each stock shows where recent support and resistance have formed from price history — computed from data, not drawn by hand.
A support level is a price where something happened before, not a guarantee it happens again.

Two opposing forces in markets. Momentum says what\'s moving tends to keep moving — trending stocks attract more buyers, and trends can persist longer than expected. Mean reversion says extreme moves tend to snap back toward an average — a stock or index that has moved very far very fast has historically been more likely to pause or reverse than to keep accelerating at the same rate.\n\nNeither is universally true. The regime matters: momentum strategies have worked better in trending macro environments; mean reversion has worked better in range-bound ones.

Every stock is classified as Momentum, Mean Reversion, Ranging, or Warning based on its current price behavior. Forward calls track how those classifications have resolved for that specific stock — the honest record of what happened next.
Which force is dominant right now. The classification names the current condition; the resolution is unknown.

Markets are forward-looking — a stock\'s price reflects what investors expect about future earnings, not just current ones. This creates a \"buy the rumor, sell the news\" dynamic: if a company reports strong earnings but the result was already expected, the stock may not move — or may fall. What moves a stock is the gap between the reported number and what was expected (\"the surprise\").\n\nStocks often move in the days before an earnings report as traders position around expectations, and then sharply at the report itself.
The fundamentals section shows the next earnings date and whether it\'s pre-market or after-close. The daily digest after a report summarizes the result and initial reaction.
How big the post-earnings move will be. Implied moves from options are one way the market prices that uncertainty — the app doesn\'t currently show this.

As the economic cycle shifts, different sectors tend to lead and lag. Early expansion: cyclicals and financials. Late expansion: energy and materials. Slowdown: healthcare and staples. Recession: utilities and consumer staples. This isn\'t a rule — it\'s a tendency, and the cycle rarely follows a clean script.\n\nThe XLY/XLP ratio (Consumer Discretionary vs. Consumer Staples) is one of the cleanest real-time reads on which direction the rotation is leaning — are investors buying wants or needs?
Consumer Rotation in the Systemic Risk gauge tracks this directly. A ratio above 1.7 (Offensive) suggests risk appetite in consumer spending; below 1.25 (Flight to Safety) suggests defense.
Where in the cycle we are — that requires combining this signal with macro, credit, and earnings data.

Not all stocks respond to rising rates the same way. Growth stocks (whose value depends heavily on future earnings) are mathematically more sensitive to rising rates — higher rates discount those future earnings more heavily, compressing their valuations. Value stocks, financials, and dividend payers tend to be less rate-sensitive or even rate-benefiting in some cases. Bonds fall in price when rates rise (a fixed coupon is worth less when new bonds pay more).\n\nThe Equity Risk Premium is the cleanest single measure of how rate moves are affecting the relative attractiveness of stocks vs. Treasuries — when it falls below 2%, bonds are offering nearly as much yield as equities, with less risk.
Fed Funds and the 10-year are in Macro Vitals (polarity inverted — rising = red). ERP is in the Valuation gauge.
Which specific stocks in your watchlist are most exposed — that requires knowing their earnings duration and leverage, which the app doesn\'t compute.

A market index can rise while most of its constituent stocks fall — if a handful of very large companies go up enough, they pull the cap-weighted index with them. This is breadth divergence: the index is up, but the average stock isn\'t. It\'s historically been read as a sign that a rally is becoming fragile — fewer stocks are participating, which means fewer buyers sustaining it.\n\nThe equal-weight vs. cap-weight comparison (RSP vs. SPY) makes this visible directly: if RSP is lagging SPY, the mega-caps are doing the work alone.
Market Breadth tracks the 1-day change in RSP/SPY. A sustained Narrowing reading (RSP consistently lagging) is more meaningful than a single day.
How long a narrow rally can persist — it can go on for months. Breadth is a condition, not a timer.

Markets move on more than fundamentals — how investors feel about risk shifts prices too, sometimes faster than the underlying data changes. A handful of indicators try to measure that feeling directly, mostly by looking at what investors are actually doing with their money rather than what they say.

• Fear & Greed and the Put/Call ratio (CNN): gauge short-term market mood. Extreme fear has historically coincided with periods where selling pressure was overdone, extreme greed with periods of elevated risk-taking — neither is a timing signal on its own, and both can stay at an extreme for a long time.
• NAAIM Exposure Index: tracks how invested active fund managers actually are, week to week — a direct measure of professional positioning rather than a survey response.
• AAII Sentiment Survey: measures individual investor sentiment (bullish/neutral/bearish) — a widely watched but famously unreliable contrarian indicator. Extreme readings in either direction are sometimes read as a sign a consensus view has gotten crowded, not as confirmation the consensus is right.
• CFTC Commitment of Traders (COT) report and FINRA short interest data: show what large futures traders and short sellers are positioned for — institutional-level positioning that moves on a different timescale than retail sentiment.

This family appears in Tactical Momentum (Fear & Greed, Put/Call) and in the Posture and Positioning gauges. Posture combines NAAIM, SqueezeMetrics\' Dark Index (DIX), and net liquidity signals; Positioning combines AAII, COT futures data, and FINRA short interest. Each is one input among several — none is used alone anywhere in the app.

Interest rates set the \"cost of money\" for the entire economy, so changes to them ripple into nearly everything else. When the Federal Reserve raises rates, borrowing gets more expensive for companies and consumers alike — which can slow spending and earnings growth, and tends to make already-established cash flows (like bonds, or stocks priced heavily on future growth) relatively more attractive than before. Rate cuts generally work in the opposite direction. Neither effect is instant or guaranteed — markets often move on the expectation of a rate change well before the change itself happens.

• 10-year and 2-year Treasury yields: the spread between them is widely watched because an inverted yield curve (short-term yields above long-term) has historically preceded economic slowdowns — though the timing and reliability of that relationship varies a lot across cycles.\n• Inflation data (CPI, core PCE): a primary input into what the Fed does next — hotter-than-expected readings tend to raise the odds of tighter policy, and vice versa.

This appears in Macro Vitals (the Fed funds rate, the 10-year yield, CPI and core PCE inflation, unemployment) and, for the yield curve, in Systemic Risk — all built from FRED data, the same source the Fed itself publishes.
Technical analysis looks at price and volume patterns themselves, on the theory that price action reflects everything the market currently knows or believes, even before that shows up elsewhere.

• Moving averages: smooth out day-to-day noise to show the underlying trend — the 50-day and 200-day are the most widely watched. Price above its 200-day average is commonly read as a sign the longer-term trend is up, below it the opposite. A \"golden cross\" (50-day crossing above the 200-day) and \"death cross\" (the reverse) are watched as longer-term trend-change signals, though both can lag the actual turn by weeks.\n• Support and resistance: price levels where a stock has repeatedly stopped falling or stopped rising in the past — the idea being that enough market participants remember those levels that they influence behavior again next time price approaches them. Neither is a hard floor or ceiling; both get broken regularly.

This is the SMA card and the momentum/trend classification on each stock\'s detail screen — computed directly from price history, not from an AI\'s read of a chart. The forward calls feature tracks how a classified setup (e.g. a momentum or mean-reversion read) actually played out over the following trading sessions — a historical record of the app\'s own calls, not a prediction of what comes next.

Valuation asks a different question than sentiment or technicals: is the price being paid reasonable relative to what the company actually earns? The P/E ratio (price divided by earnings per share) is the most common starting point — a \"high\" P/E means the market is paying more per dollar of current earnings, often because it expects faster future growth; a \"low\" P/E can mean the opposite, or that the market has real concerns the price hasn\'t priced out.

• Sector-relative P/E: comparing a stock\'s P/E to its own sector, rather than to the market as a whole, controls for the fact that some industries structurally trade at higher multiples than others (growth software vs. utilities, for example) — a stock that looks \"cheap\" against the whole market can be expensive against its actual peers, and vice versa.\n• Low valuation isn\'t automatically a bargain: it\'s frequently a sign the market has already priced in a real risk. Valuation is one lens among several, not a standalone verdict.

This is the sector-relative P/E metric on each stock\'s fundamentals — the stock\'s own P/E measured against its sector\'s median, computed from the same underlying data as the headline P/E figure, not a separate estimate.
